slides.title: Form A: item 1
slides.html:
Triangle TUV ≅ triangle HJK. Which side matches UV, and which angle matches angle T?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Side JK and angle H, by the ordered correspondence.

Reveal second check

slides.title: Form A: item 2
slides.html:
Triangle LMN ≅ triangle CBA, LM = 7a - 6, and CB = 57. Find a and LM.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

LM=CB by CPCTC, so 7a-6=57, 7a=63, a=9 and LM=57.

Reveal second check

7(9)-6=57. L↔C and M↔B check the matched endpoints.

slides.title: Form A: item 3
slides.html:
HI = RS = 8, HJ = RT = 13, and angle IHJ = angle SRT = 37 degrees. Prove triangle HIJ ≅ triangle RST. Then show IJ = ST.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The two side pairs and their included angles match, so HIJ≅RST by SAS. Then IJ=ST by CPCTC.

Reveal second check

The side endpoints share H and R, the marked angle vertices. A ray-alignment rigid motion fixes I to S and J to T.

slides.title: Form A: item 4
slides.html:
Triangles UVW and DFE have angle V = angle F = 48 degrees, angle W = angle E = 73 degrees, and VW = FE = 12. Prove the triangles are congruent. Which side matches UW?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

VW and FE are included sides between the marked angles, so UVW≅DFE by ASA. UW matches DE.

Reveal second check

V↔F and W↔E fix the base endpoints; the two endpoint rays intersect uniquely, forcing U↔D.

slides.title: Form A: item 5
slides.html:
Segments JK and LN meet at O, the midpoint of both. JO = 4 and LO = 9. Prove triangle JOL ≅ triangle KON. Then give KO and NO.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

JO=KO=4 and LO=NO=9 by midpoint. Angle JOL=KON by vertical angles. JOL≅KON by SAS.

Reveal second check

A half-turn about O exchanges J,K and L,N; it preserves all distances and gives the same congruence.

slides.title: Form A: item 6
slides.html:
Triangle FGH ≅ triangle UTS. Angle G = (3c + 8) degrees and angle T = 50 degrees. Find c and give the reason for your equation.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

G↔T, so 3c+8=50 by CPCTC. Hence 3c=42 and c=14.

Reveal second check

3(14)+8=50; the second letters in FGH and UTS match.

slides.title: Form A: item 7
slides.html:
In triangle PQR, PQ = PR, angle Q = (2e + 14) degrees, and angle R = (5e - 16) degrees. Find e and each base angle.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The isosceles theorem gives 2e+14=5e-16. Thus 3e=30, e=10 and both base angles are 34 degrees.

Reveal second check

2(10)+14=34 and 5(10)-16=34, with positive equal legs possible. Do not compute the apex angle.

slides.title: Form A: item 8
slides.html:
Triangle VXW has angle X = angle W, VX = 3g + 4, and VW = g + 32. Prove the legs are equal without using the converse theorem. Then find g and the leg length.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Compare VXW and VWX. The base-angle pairs match and XW=WX; ASA gives congruence and CPCTC gives VX=VW. Solve 3g+4=g+32, so g=14 and each leg is 46.

Reveal second check

3(14)+4=46=14+32. Also the established converse isosceles theorem directly gives the same leg equality.

slides.title: Form A: item 9
slides.html:
Triangles ABC and UVW have matching angles of 42, 58 and 80 degrees, in that order. AB = 6 and UV = 15. Explain why AAA can't prove they are congruent, even if you match the corners a different way.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The unique equal-angle matching is A↔U, B↔V, C↔W. It would require AB=UV, but 6≠15, so the triangles are not congruent.

Reveal second check

Rigid motions preserve lengths, and the distinct angle sizes forbid any different vertex matching. The angle equalities are givens, not an inference from equilateral triangles.

slides.title: Form A: item 10
slides.html:
In convex quadrilateral KLMN, KL = KN and LM = NM. A proof starts with 'angle LKM = angle NKM by CPCTC.' Fix the proof so it shows KM bisects angle LKN.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

First KM=KM by reflexivity. With KL=KN and LM=NM, KLM≅KNM by SSS. Now angle LKM=NKM by CPCTC. In a convex quadrilateral the diagonal KM lies inside angle LKN, so it bisects that angle.

Reveal second check

K↔K, L↔N, M↔M matches each of the three side facts. Both equal angles are the two parts of the original angle, not exterior angles.

geo.check: K↔K, L↔N, M↔M matches each of the three side facts. Both equal angles are the two parts of the original angle, not exterior angles.

slides.title: Form A: item 11
slides.html:
E and F are 14 units apart. Circles of radius 10 centered at E and F cross at G and H, on opposite sides of EF. Prove triangle EFG ≅ triangle EFH. Would radius 7 give two crossing points for the perpendicular bisector construction?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

EG=EH=10 and FG=FH=10 by equal radii; EF=EF, so EFG≅EFH by SSS. Radius 7 gives tangency at the midpoint, not two points, because 7+7=14. The perpendicular-bisector construction needs radius greater than 7.

Reveal second check

Reflection across EF fixes the centers and swaps G,H.

slides.title: Form A: item 12
slides.html:
Use the figure. Q1 and Q2 are on the same ray from O. OP = 10, OQ1 = 2 and OQ2 = 10. Both Q points lie on one circle centered at P. Prove that triangles OPQ1 and OPQ2 have matching SSA parts but are not congruent. Don't use trig or the distance formula.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

OP is common, PQ1=PQ2 as radii of the same circle, and angle POQ1=POQ2 because OQ1,OQ2 are the same ray. This angle is not included between OP and PQ. The third sides are 2 and 10, so the named correspondence fails congruence.

Reveal second check

Writing the unknown radius as r, the perimeters are 12+r and 20+r, unequal. Thus no other correspondence can make the triangles congruent.

slides.title: Form B: item 7
slides.html:
In triangle STU, ST = SU, angle T = (4f - 11) degrees, and angle U = (2f + 15) degrees. Find f and each base angle.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The isosceles theorem gives 4f-11=2f+15. Hence 2f=26, f=13, and both base angles are 41 degrees.

Reveal second check

4(13)-11=41 and 2(13)+15=41. The base-angle theorem, not an angle-sum calculation, supplies the equation.

Triangle HIK has angle I = angle K, HI = 5h - 8, and HK = 2h + 43. Prove the legs are equal without using the converse theorem. Then find h and the leg length.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

Reveal second check

5(17)-8=77=2(17)+43. The proved converse isosceles theorem is an independent direct check of the equality.

slides.title: Form B: item 9
slides.html:
Triangles DEF and LMN have matching angles of 36, 63 and 81 degrees, in that order. DE = 8 and LM = 20. Explain why AAA can't prove they are congruent, even if you match the corners a different way.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

The unique equal-angle matching is D↔L, E↔M, F↔N. Congruence would require DE=LM; 8≠20 rules it out.

Reveal second check

Any isometry preserves the given side length. Because the angle sizes are distinct, permuting vertices cannot bypass that mismatch.

slides.title: Form B: item 10
slides.html:
In convex quadrilateral RSTU, RS = RU and ST = UT. A proof starts with 'angle SRT = angle URT by CPCTC.' Fix the proof so it shows RT bisects angle SRU.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

First RT=RT by reflexivity. Then RST≅RUT by SSS using the two given pairs. CPCTC gives angle SRT=URT. Convexity puts RT inside angle SRU, hence RT is its bisector.

Reveal second check

The ordered match R↔R, S↔U, T↔T makes all three SSS equalities corresponding. The conclusion occurs only after congruence.

slides.title: Form B: item 11
slides.html:
G and H are 18 units apart. Circles of radius 12 centered at G and H cross at J and K, on opposite sides of GH. Prove triangle GHJ ≅ triangle GHK. Would radius 9 give two crossing points for the perpendicular bisector construction?

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

GJ=GK=12 and HJ=HK=12 by equal radii; GH=GH, so GHJ≅GHK by SSS. Radius 9 gives tangency, since 9+9=18. Two intersections require radius greater than 9.

Reveal second check

Reflection across GH exchanges J,K.

slides.title: Form B: item 12
slides.html:
Use the figure. N1 and N2 are on the same ray from L. LM = 17, LN1 = 5 and LN2 = 11. Both N points lie on one circle centered at M. Prove that triangles LMN1 and LMN2 have matching SSA parts but are not congruent. Don't use trig or the distance formula.

Try it on paper first, then reveal.

Reveal solution

LM is shared; MN1=MN2 as radii of one circle; angle MLN1=MLN2 because both N points are on the same ray from L. That angle is nonincluded for LM and MN. LN1=5 differs from LN2=11, ruling out the named congruence.

Reveal second check

With unknown common radius r, perimeters 22+r and 28+r differ, so no alternative correspondence works either.
